hops.title: Why your own touch tickles less
hops.text: Run a fingertip lightly across your own palm, then have a friend do the same. Self-touch is reliably rated less ticklish. In 1998, Sarah-Jayne Blakemore and colleagues scanned volunteers during both. Self-touch produced less activity in somatosensory cortex, and the cerebellum was less active when a movement produced a touch than when it did not. The authors read this as the cerebellum predicting the sensory result of your own movement and sending a signal that cancels the response. A year later, volunteers' left hands moved a robot arm that drove a second robot stroking the right palm. As delay or angle error grew, tickliness ratings rose.

sources.citation: Blakemore SJ, Wolpert DM, Frith CD. Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation. Nature Neuroscience. 1998;1(7):635-640.
Blakemore SJ, Frith CD, Wolpert DM. Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience. 1999;11(5):551-559.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student at a desk lightly running a fingertip across their own open palm while a friend's hand reaches in.
image.caption: Your brain predicts the feel of your own touch and turns the response down, so self-touch tickles less.

hops.title: Astronauts' brain ventricles enlarge in orbit
hops.text: Months in orbit enlarge the fluid-filled spaces inside an astronaut's brain. Researchers scanned eleven cosmonauts before and after long missions and found that their lateral ventricles had grown by an average of 13.3 percent and their third ventricle by 10.4 percent. The authors point to slower absorption of cerebrospinal fluid in microgravity as the likely cause. Seven months after landing, the ventricles still had not shrunk all the way back. A later study of thirty astronauts suggested that most of the growth happens in the first six months, and that crews who flew again within three years showed little new enlargement, perhaps because they had not fully recovered.

sources.citation: Van Ombergen A, Jillings S, Jeurissen B, et al. Brain ventricular volume changes induced by long-duration spaceflight. PNAS. 2019;116(21):10531-10536.
McGregor HR, Hupfeld KE, Pasternak O, et al. Impacts of spaceflight experience on human brain structure. Scientific Reports. 2023;13(1):7878.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An astronaut floating upside down inside a space station module beside a window looking out at Earth.
image.caption: Some brain ventricles stay larger for months after a long spaceflight; slower absorption of cerebrospinal fluid is the likely cause.

hops.afterHeading: From where to what: four kinds of evidence
hops.title: A dead salmon in an fMRI scanner
hops.text: One spring morning in 2005, Craig Bennett bought a whole Atlantic salmon at a supermarket, eighteen inches and 3.8 pounds, and put it in an fMRI scanner. The dead fish was shown fifteen photos of people and asked what each person was feeling. In 2008 his team analysed the scans, testing 8,064 voxels, the small cubes an fMRI image is built from, each against a strict cutoff but with no allowance for the number of tests. Sixteen came up active, including a cluster in the salmon's brain cavity. Corrected for the number of tests, none survived. Noise alone made a dead fish look like it was thinking.

sources.citation: Bennett CM, Baird AA, Miller MB, Wolford GL. Neural correlates of interspecies perspective taking in the post-mortem Atlantic Salmon: An argument for multiple comparisons correction. OHBM 2009 poster.
Bennett CM, Wolford GL, Miller MB. The principled control of false positives in neuroimaging. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. 2009;4(4):417-422.
Bennett CM. The story behind the Atlantic salmon. prefrontal.org blog, September 2009.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A whole silver salmon resting on a padded tray at the entrance of a white ring-shaped scanner.
image.caption: Without correcting for thousands of tests, random scanner noise lit up a dead salmon's brain cavity.
